unit.name: Working in Construction
unit.subtitle: Construction trades and careers, health and safety law, and working safely on site.

lessons.title: Construction Trades and Careers
lessons.description: The main construction trades, what each tradesperson does, and the safety regulations they follow.
lessons.content_html:
The World of Construction Trades

Construction is one of the largest and most diverse industries in the UK. Rather than one single job, the sector is made up of many skilled trades — each responsible for a different part of a building project. Whether constructing a new house or restoring a historic church, skilled tradespeople work from plans and specifications and follow safety regulations throughout. Understanding what each trade does is essential for anyone entering the industry.

Bricklaying

A bricklayer builds walls and structures from bricks or blocks. They work from drawings and written specifications, spreading layers of mortar and carefully placing each brick or block in position. After laying each course, the bricklayer checks that the work is perfectly horizontal (level) and vertical (plumb) using a spirit level. Walls are laid in traditional bonding patterns — such as stretcher bond or English bond — which distribute the load and give the structure strength. Correct bonding also produces a neat, professional finish.

Stonemasonry

A stonemason works with natural stone rather than manufactured bricks. They dress (shape) stone blocks using chisels and other specialist tools, and carve decorative features such as window surrounds, cornices and column capitals. Stonemasons also construct dry-stone walling — walls built without mortar that are common in rural areas — and repair and clean the stone mouldings and ornamental features found on older and historic buildings. This trade is closely linked to heritage conservation work.

Plastering

A plasterer applies wet finishes and protective coverings to both internal and external surfaces. On the outside of a building, the plasterer applies render to protect the masonry from weather. Inside, they skim walls and ceilings with a smooth coat of finishing plaster. Plasterers also carry out dry lining — fixing plasterboard sheets to internal stud walls as an alternative to wet plaster — which is a fast, common method in modern construction. Skilled plasterers can also replicate traditional ornamental plasterwork, using moulds and casts to produce decorative ceiling roses and cornices for heritage projects.

Key Fact

Plasterers work on external walls (render), internal walls and ceilings (wet plaster skim), internal studs (dry lining with plasterboard), and heritage features (ornamental plasterwork using moulds and casts).

Carpentry and Joinery

Carpentry and joinery are related but distinct trades. A joiner works primarily in a workshop, cutting and joining pieces of timber to make components such as doors, window frames, staircases and fitted furniture. These items are then delivered to site. A carpenter works on site, installing the components the joiner has made, as well as structural timber elements including floor joists, floorboards and roof trusses. Carpenters also construct wall partitions, fit interior woodwork such as skirting boards and kitchen units, and can replicate traditional ornamental mouldings. The key distinction is simple: joiners make components in the workshop; carpenters fix them on site.

On a typical housing project, a joiner in a timber yard would cut, assemble and finish a staircase off site, ensuring every tread and riser is precisely made to the architect's drawings. The carpenter would then take that finished staircase to the building and fix it securely in position, fitting handrails, balusters and nosings. The same split applies to kitchens: the joiner makes the carcasses and drawer boxes; the carpenter installs them level and plumb, trims worktops and hangs doors. In exam questions, always use the correct term — do not call a site-based tradesperson a "joiner" or a workshop-based one a "carpenter".

Electrical Installation

An electrician installs, inspects and tests electrical services and equipment throughout a building. This includes running cables, fitting consumer units (fuse boards), wiring sockets, switches, lighting circuits and specialist equipment such as security systems or fire alarms. Electricians must follow relevant safety regulations at all times — electrical faults are a leading cause of serious injury and fire on construction sites. All electrical installation work in the UK must comply with BS 7671 (the IET Wiring Regulations), and qualified electricians are responsible for testing and certifying that the work is safe before a building is occupied.

Plumbing Installation

A plumber installs the systems that supply and remove water in a building. This covers cold-water and hot-water supply, sanitation systems (toilets, basins and baths), boilers, and central heating pipework and radiators. Plumbers follow safety regulations relevant to their trade — for example, any work on gas appliances or gas pipework must be carried out by a person registered with Gas Safe, the UK's official gas safety register. As well as pipework, plumbers also install traditional lead flashings and lead roof coverings on heritage buildings, making the skill set broader than most people realise.

Key Fact

Plumbers install cold water, hot water, sanitation, boilers and central heating. Any work on gas systems must be carried out by a Gas Safe registered engineer — this is a legal requirement. Plumbers also install lead flashings and roof coverings.

Painting and Decorating

A painter and decorator prepares and applies paint, wallpaper and other decorative finishes to interior surfaces. On the outside of a building, they apply paint and protective finishes to external surfaces such as rendered walls, timber windows, doors and metalwork. Preparation is a major part of the role — this includes sanding, filling, priming and masking before any finish is applied. Like all construction trades, painters and decorators must follow relevant safety regulations, particularly when working at height on ladders or scaffolding, or when using chemical strippers and solvent-based paints.

Flooring and Tiling

A floor layer (sometimes called a floor and wall tiler) carries out a range of finishing tasks. They prepare surfaces using levelling compounds to create a flat, even base before any finish is applied. Once the subfloor is ready, they lay carpet and vinyl floor finishes, cutting and fixing them neatly to the walls and around obstacles. They also install ceramic wall and floor tiles in kitchens, bathrooms and other wet areas, mixing and applying adhesive and grout to the correct depth. Getting the preparation right is crucial — uneven subfloors cause tiles to crack and carpet to ripple over time.

Every tradesperson on a construction project works from a set of architect's drawings and a written specification. The drawings show dimensions, layouts and details; the written spec document describes the materials, standards and methods to be used. Working from these documents ensures that every trade delivers work that fits with the other trades' work — for example, a plumber must position pipework precisely where the architect has planned so that the plasterer can board over it and the tiler can finish around it. Safety regulations, such as Building Regulations and manufacturer's guidance, are also followed throughout, protecting workers, future occupants and the general public. Without this shared framework, buildings would not be safe or fit for purpose.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The most common mistake in trade questions is confusing carpenters and joiners, or confusing the plumber's role with the electrician's. Learn the joiner/carpenter split precisely: joiners make components in a workshop; carpenters fix them on site. For gas work, always name Gas Safe as the required registration — writing "a qualified person" alone is not specific enough to earn the mark. In extended-answer questions about roles and responsibilities, link each trade's work back to following plans, specifications and safety regulations, as this shows understanding of how the industry is organised.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Construction is made up of specialist trades: bricklaying, stonemasonry, plastering, carpentry and joinery, electrical installation, plumbing, painting and decorating, and flooring and tiling.
  • A joiner makes timber components in a workshop; a carpenter installs them on site — this distinction is frequently tested in exams.
  • All trades work from plans and specifications and must follow safety regulations relevant to their work — for example, Gas Safe registration for plumbers working with gas, and BS 7671 compliance for electricians.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the role of a stonemason?
A) Laying bricks in mortar using traditional bonding patterns
B) Dressing, carving and laying natural stone, including dry-stone walling
C) Applying levelling compounds and laying carpet and vinyl floor finishes
D) Installing cold water, hot water and central heating systems
practice_questions.marks: B) Dressing, carving and laying natural stone, including dry-stone walling [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two tasks carried out by a plasterer on a construction project.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct tasks from: applying render to external walls / applying plaster to inside walls and ceilings / dry lining internal stud walls (plasterboard) / replicating traditional ornamental plasterwork using moulds and casts. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a joiner and a carpenter.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying that they are different roles (e.g. "they are separate trades"). A second mark for explaining the joiner's role (e.g. "a joiner works in a workshop, joining pieces of wood to make components such as doors, window frames or staircases"). A third mark for explaining the carpenter's role (e.g. "a carpenter works on site, installing the components made by the joiner and also fitting structural elements such as floor joists, floorboards and roof trusses"). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the work of an electrician on a new-build house, including one safety regulation they must follow.
practice_questions.marks:
Description of work (up to 3 marks): installs, inspects and tests electrical services and equipment; runs cables and fits consumer units (fuse boards); wires sockets, switches and lighting circuits; may install specialist equipment such as security systems or fire alarms (one mark per distinct point, up to 3).
Safety regulation (1 mark): for example, must comply with BS 7671 (the IET Wiring Regulations) and certify that completed work is safe before the building is occupied. [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A construction firm is building a new residential estate. The site manager notices that gas boilers need to be fitted, but the assigned plumber is not Gas Safe registered.

Explain why this is a problem and what action the site manager should take.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A clear explanation that Gas Safe registration is a legal requirement for anyone working on gas appliances or pipework in the UK; using an unregistered person is illegal, creates serious safety risks (including carbon monoxide poisoning, gas leaks or explosion), and could expose the employer to legal liability. The site manager should stop the plumber from carrying out any gas work immediately and arrange for a Gas Safe registered engineer to carry out the installation. Marks also available for noting that the site manager is responsible for safety on site and may be held to account for breaches.
Secure (3-4 marks): Recognises Gas Safe as a legal requirement, identifies safety risks and states an appropriate action.
Developing (2 marks): Identifies Gas Safe as important but limited explanation of why.
Emerging (1 mark): A single basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A historic manor house is being restored. The project requires bricklayers, stonemasons, carpenters and painters and decorators.

Evaluate the importance of each trade working from plans and specifications on this type of project, compared with a standard new-build.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A developed evaluation covering how plans and specifications ensure trades coordinate their work (e.g. carpenter's components are sized to fit the stonemason's openings; painter's specification details heritage-approved finishes). On a heritage project this is especially important because materials and methods must match the existing fabric of the building, comply with planning conditions, and often satisfy conservation requirements — errors are harder and more expensive to correct than on a standard new-build. Counter-argument: on a standard new-build the same framework applies but tolerances are less critical and materials are more standardised. Substantiated judgement: following plans and specifications is critical on all projects, but the consequences of deviation are more severe on a heritage project. Quality of written communication should be credited.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two trades discussed with some comparison of heritage vs new-build.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points, largely descriptive.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points with little development. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which tradesperson joins pieces of wood in a workshop to make components such as doors and window frames?

lessons.title: Health and Safety Law and Risk
lessons.description: Construction site hazards, risk assessments, and the legislation employers must follow to protect workers.
lessons.content_html:
Why Construction Sites Are Hazardous

Construction is consistently ranked among the most dangerous industries in the UK. Workers, employers and members of the public can all be placed at risk on or near a building site, and understanding those risks is the first step towards controlling them. Every person on site — from the site manager to the newest apprentice — must understand the hazards they face and the rules that exist to protect them.

Risks on Construction Sites

Employees working on construction sites face four main categories of risk. First, heavy plant and construction vehicles — such as excavators, dumper trucks and mobile cranes — move around sites carrying heavy loads. A worker in a vehicle's blind spot faces a serious risk of being struck or crushed. Second, working at height is one of the leading causes of death in construction; falling from a scaffold, ladder or unguarded edge can result in fatal injuries. Third, manual handling — lifting, carrying, pushing or pulling heavy or awkward loads — causes a high proportion of musculoskeletal injuries in the industry. Fourth, slips, trips and falls on level ground — caused by wet surfaces, trailing cables or uneven ground — are among the most frequent causes of workplace injury on site.

Employers have a legal responsibility for the safe operation of construction sites. They are accountable for the systems, equipment and procedures in place, and can be prosecuted or fined in the event of accidents or incidents. Members of the public can also be put at risk when close to an active construction site — from falling objects, site traffic emerging onto public roads, and hazardous materials such as cement dust or asbestos. Sites must be securely fenced and clearly signed to prevent unauthorised access by members of the public, including children.

Key Fact

The four main risks to employees on construction sites are: heavy plant and construction vehicles, working at height, manual handling, and slips, trips and falls. Employers are legally responsible for site safety and can be prosecuted if accidents occur. The public must be protected from site traffic, falling objects and hazardous materials.

Following Correct Procedures

Simply knowing about hazards is not enough — everyone on site must follow the correct procedures. Procedures are the documented rules and steps that ensure contractors and employees work safely and prevent accidents. Examples include signing in and out of site, wearing the correct personal protective equipment in designated areas, following a specific method statement for a task, and attending site induction briefings. When procedures are ignored — for example, removing safety barriers around a floor opening to carry materials more easily — the risk of a serious accident increases significantly.

Risk Assessments

A risk assessment is a formal examination of the hazards associated with a task or workplace, and the control measures needed to reduce risk to an acceptable level. There are two types relevant to construction. A general risk assessment covers the overall health and safety hazards present on the site — such as access routes, site housekeeping, fire escape routes and general site traffic. A specific risk assessment is written for a particular hazardous activity, such as working at height on a scaffold, carrying out manual handling of heavy blocks, or working in a noisy environment. Both types must identify the hazard, assess who might be harmed and how, and set out appropriate control measures.

A control measure is any action, barrier or system that reduces the risk of harm. Effective control measures are chosen by following the hierarchy of control — a priority order that tries to eliminate or reduce the hazard at source before relying on personal protective equipment (PPE) as a last resort. At the top of the hierarchy: eliminate the hazard if possible (e.g. design out the need to work at height by pre-assembling components at ground level). Next: substitute the hazard with something safer (e.g. use a less hazardous chemical). Then: engineering controls such as guarding or extraction systems; administrative controls such as safe systems of work and limited working hours; and finally PPE. Examiners expect students to understand that PPE is the last line of defence, not the first choice.

Health and Safety at Work Act

The Health and Safety at Work Act (1974) is the cornerstone of workplace safety law in the UK. It places clear duties on employers to protect the health, safety and welfare of workers, visitors and members of the public. Under this Act, employers in construction are legally required to prepare risk assessments, decide what control measures are necessary, and prevent or control exposure to hazards. They must also ensure that the hierarchy of control is followed when selecting those measures, monitor the level of exposure to hazards over time, prepare accident procedures so that incidents are dealt with promptly and correctly, and provide adequate training and supervision to all employees so they can carry out their work safely.

Key Fact

Under the Health and Safety at Work Act, employers must: prepare risk assessments; decide on control measures; prevent or control exposure to hazards; follow the hierarchy of control; monitor exposure levels; have accident procedures in place; and train and supervise employees.

COSHH Regulations

The Control of Substances Hazardous to Health (COSHH) regulations sit alongside the Health and Safety at Work Act and deal specifically with hazardous substances. Construction sites contain many substances that can harm health — including cement dust (which can cause dermatitis and respiratory disease), silica dust from cutting stone or concrete (which causes a serious lung disease called silicosis), solvent fumes from adhesives and paints, and asbestos fibres in older buildings. Under COSHH, employers must identify hazardous substances on site, assess the risk they pose, and put in place control measures to prevent or reduce workers' exposure. This might mean using safer substitute products, providing local exhaust ventilation, or supplying appropriate PPE such as dust masks or gloves.

Respirable crystalline silica (RCS) is released when cutting, grinding or drilling materials that contain silica — including concrete, stone, brick and mortar. The particles are extremely fine and invisible to the naked eye, meaning a worker can inhale a dangerous amount without realising it. Over time, silica dust causes silicosis — permanent and irreversible scarring of the lungs that reduces breathing capacity and can be fatal. It is also linked to lung cancer. Because the damage occurs slowly, workers may not notice symptoms for years. COSHH assessments for any cutting or grinding task must identify RCS as a hazard, and control measures typically include wet cutting (using water to suppress dust), on-tool extraction, and where necessary a suitable dust mask rated for RCS (a P3 or FFP3 standard). The insidious nature of silica dust makes COSHH compliance critically important in construction.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on legislation often ask you to name the Act or regulations and state what they require employers to do. Always name the Health and Safety at Work Act specifically — do not write "health and safety law" alone, as this is too vague to earn the mark. Similarly, name COSHH when the question involves hazardous substances such as dust, fumes or chemicals. For risk assessment questions, make sure you distinguish between general (whole-site) and specific (task-level) assessments, and always relate control measures back to the hierarchy — eliminating or reducing the hazard at source is always preferable to relying on PPE.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Construction sites carry significant risks for employees (heavy plant, working at height, manual handling, slips/trips/falls), employers (legal accountability) and the public (site traffic, falling objects, hazardous materials).
  • Risk assessments — both general (whole-site) and specific (task-level) — identify hazards and set out control measures to reduce risk, following the hierarchy of control.
  • The Health and Safety at Work Act requires employers to assess risks, implement control measures, monitor hazards, prepare accident procedures, and train and supervise workers. COSHH regulations add specific duties around hazardous substances such as dust and fumes.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a specific risk assessment on a construction site?
A) A general check of all site access routes and emergency exits
B) An assessment of manual handling tasks involved in lifting heavy concrete blocks
C) A review of the site's overall fire evacuation procedure
D) An inspection of the site perimeter fencing
practice_questions.marks: B) An assessment of manual handling tasks involved in lifting heavy concrete blocks [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two risks that employees face on a construction site.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: heavy plant and construction vehicles / working at height / manual handling / slips, trips and falls. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why employers on a construction site must follow the hierarchy of control when selecting control measures.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying that the hierarchy of control is a priority order for selecting control measures. A second mark for explaining the principle (e.g. it requires employers to try to eliminate or reduce the hazard at source before relying on less reliable measures). A third mark for development (e.g. PPE is at the bottom of the hierarchy because it relies on individual workers wearing it correctly at all times, which cannot be guaranteed, whereas engineering controls such as guarding protect everyone automatically). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the employer duties required by the Health and Safety at Work Act on a construction project.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any four distinct duties from: prepare risk assessments / decide on control measures / prevent or control exposure to hazards / ensure the hierarchy of control is followed / monitor exposure to hazards / prepare procedures to deal with accidents / train and supervise employees. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Workers on a construction site are cutting stone blocks using dry angle grinders. The site manager has not carried out a COSHH assessment for this task.

Explain the risks this creates and what the site manager should do to comply with COSHH regulations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Identifies the specific hazardous substance (silica dust / respirable crystalline silica released when cutting stone); explains the health risk (silicosis — irreversible lung scarring, lung cancer); explains why the absence of a COSHH assessment is a legal breach; states what the site manager must do (carry out a COSHH assessment identifying RCS as a hazard and implement control measures such as wet cutting, on-tool extraction ventilation, and appropriate PPE such as FFP3 dust masks). Marks also available for noting that COSHH sits alongside the Health and Safety at Work Act and that the employer can be prosecuted for non-compliance.
Secure (3-4 marks): Identifies the hazardous substance, names the health risk and states one or more appropriate actions.
Developing (2 marks): Identifies a hazardous substance or health risk but limited explanation.
Emerging (1 mark): A single basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A new housing development site has had three accidents in one month: a worker slipped on a wet walkway, a delivery driver struck a worker near the site entrance, and a labourer sustained a back injury lifting heavy blocks.

Evaluate how effective risk assessments and the correct hierarchy of control could have prevented these accidents.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Analyses each accident in terms of the risk assessment process and hierarchy of control. For slips/trips: a general site risk assessment should have identified wet walkways; control measures higher in the hierarchy than PPE (e.g. non-slip matting, drainage channels, clear housekeeping rules) should have been implemented before issuing wet-weather footwear. For the vehicle strike: a specific risk assessment for site traffic should have identified pedestrian/vehicle conflict; engineering controls (separate pedestrian and vehicle routes, physical barriers, banksmen) should have been in place. For the manual handling injury: a specific manual handling assessment should have identified the weight and awkwardness of concrete blocks; elimination (using mechanical aids such as a block grab) or reduction (team lifting, reduced block sizes) should have been selected before PPE. A substantiated judgement: well-conducted risk assessments, following the hierarchy from eliminate/substitute down to PPE, would have significantly reduced the likelihood of all three accidents. However, risk assessments are only effective if monitored and enforced — procedures alone are insufficient.
Secure (5-6 marks): Two accidents discussed with reference to risk assessment and hierarchy. Some applied evaluation.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points, mostly descriptive.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points, little development. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is the primary piece of UK legislation placing duties on employers to protect the health, safety and welfare of all employees and others in the workplace?
options: The Health and Safety at Work Act
The Construction, Design and Management Regulations

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of risk assessment covers the overall health and safety hazards present across a construction site, such as access routes and general site traffic?
Cutting or grinding concrete and stone releases fine _____ dust, which can cause silicosis — irreversible scarring of the lungs.
In the hierarchy of control, _____ is the last line of defence and should only be used when higher-level measures are not reasonably practicable.

lessons.title: Working Safely on Site
lessons.description: Selecting and using PPE correctly, safe working with services, and risks at height or in enclosed spaces.
lessons.content_html:
Protecting Workers in Practice

Knowing the law is one thing — putting it into practice every day on site is another. Three of the most critical areas of practical safety on a construction site are the correct use of personal protective equipment (PPE), following safe procedures when working with gas, water and electricity, and managing the very serious risks that arise when working at height or in enclosed spaces. Each area has its own rules, and understanding them is essential for anyone working in the construction industry.

Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)

PPE is the last line of defence in the hierarchy of control — it is used when other measures cannot fully eliminate or reduce a hazard. Employers have three key duties in relation to PPE. First, they must assess whether PPE is needed as a control measure for a given task. This means reviewing the risk assessment and identifying whether the remaining hazard (after other controls have been applied) still poses a risk to health or safety that PPE can reduce. Second, they must ensure the correct PPE is selected for the task. Different hazards require different PPE — for example, working in a dusty environment requires a suitable dust mask (not a general paper mask), while handling chemicals requires chemical-resistant gloves rather than standard cotton ones. Common types of PPE used on construction sites include hard hats (protection against falling objects), high-visibility vests (to be seen by plant operators), safety boots with steel toe-caps, eye protection, hearing protection and respiratory protection.

Third, employers must train and supervise employees in the correct use, storage and maintenance of PPE. A hard hat that is worn on the back of the head does not protect the wearer. A dust mask that is not fitted to the face properly allows hazardous particles in. PPE that is stored incorrectly — for example, safety goggles left where they can be scratched — may become ineffective. Workers must know how to fit their PPE correctly, when it must be replaced, and how to report damaged or missing equipment. Supervision ensures that PPE is actually worn consistently, not just carried on site.

Key Fact

Employer duties regarding PPE: assess whether PPE is required as a control measure; select the correct PPE for the specific hazard; train and supervise employees in the correct use, storage and maintenance of PPE. PPE that is incorrectly fitted, stored or maintained provides little or no protection.

Working Safely with Gas, Water and Electricity

Gas, water and electricity are the three services that run through almost every building, and each one presents specific risks during construction and maintenance. The fundamental rule is that gas and electricity must only be worked on by a competent person who holds the necessary qualifications and accreditations. For gas work, this means being registered with Gas Safe — it is illegal for an unregistered person to carry out any work on gas appliances or pipework. For electrical installation, inspection and testing, the relevant accreditation scheme is NICEIC (the National Inspection Council for Electrical Installation Contracting), which provides evidence that the electrician is competent and their work meets required safety standards.

Regardless of the type of service, workers must follow appropriate working practices, safety procedures and precautions at all times. The most important of these is isolation — knowing how to cut off the supply of gas, water or electricity before starting any work. For electricity, this means switching off the relevant circuit at the consumer unit and using a lock-out/tag-out procedure to prevent the circuit being accidentally re-energised while work is in progress. For gas, it means turning off the gas at the meter or at the relevant isolation valve. For water, it means closing the relevant stop valve. Failing to isolate a service before working on it is one of the most common causes of serious accidents involving services on construction sites. The correct PPE must also be used — for example, insulated tools and rubber gloves when working near live electrical components.

Isolation means cutting off the energy source before starting work. Without isolation, a live electrical cable can deliver a fatal electric shock; an un-isolated gas pipe, once cut, will release gas that can build up and ignite; an un-isolated water pipe will flood the work area when opened. Isolation does not just protect the person doing the work — it also protects anyone else on site who might be nearby or who might unknowingly switch on a circuit. A lock-out/tag-out system is the engineering control used to prevent re-energisation: the isolation point is physically locked in the off position and tagged with the name of the person working on the system, so no one else can accidentally restore the supply.

Working at Height

Working at height is defined as any work where a person could fall a distance that could cause personal injury — including working on roofs, scaffolds, ladders and mezzanine floors. It is one of the most common causes of fatal accidents in the construction industry. To ensure safety, work at height must be properly planned before it starts: the type of access equipment must be chosen in advance, competent people must be selected for the task, and the work must be organised to minimise the time spent at height and the number of people involved.

Workers at height must use an appropriate method of access. A MEWP (Mobile Elevating Work Platform) such as a cherry picker or scissor lift is often the safest option for short-duration tasks in accessible locations. Scaffold is used for longer-duration tasks and provides a stable working platform with edge protection (guardrails and toe-boards). An access platform such as a tower scaffold or podium step can be used for lower-level work. Weather conditions must always be considered — wind can destabilise lightweight platforms and make surfaces slippery; work at height should be suspended in high winds or icy conditions. All equipment used at height must be inspected regularly by a competent person before and during use, particularly scaffold, which must be inspected at least every seven days. Workers must also control risks from fragile surfaces (such as roof lights and asbestos-cement sheeting) by using crawling boards and edge protection, and from falling objects by using toe-boards, debris netting and exclusion zones at ground level below the work area.

Key Fact

When working at height: plan the work properly before starting; choose the correct access method (MEWP, scaffold or access platform); check weather conditions; use inspected equipment; and control risks from fragile surfaces and falling objects. All these measures are required — not just some of them.

Working in Enclosed Spaces

An enclosed space is any area that is fully or partially enclosed, not designed for people to work in on a regular basis, and where there is a foreseeable risk of serious injury or death. On construction sites, enclosed spaces include manholes, culverts, storage tanks, sewers, ductwork and deep excavations. Working in these locations introduces a range of hazards that do not exist in open environments.

The main risks in enclosed spaces are: exposure to fumes from solvents, adhesives or welding, which can build up to dangerous concentrations in a confined area; reduced oxygen levels caused by oxygen being displaced or consumed by chemical reactions or decaying organic matter, which can cause rapid unconsciousness and death with no warning; flooding or drowning if water enters the space suddenly; fire and explosive atmospheres from the build-up of flammable gases such as methane from decomposing waste; and entrapment in machinery or by unstable ground or structure. Workers must use atmospheric monitoring equipment to test air quality before entering and while working, and must wear appropriate PPE such as breathing apparatus if oxygen levels or gas concentrations are hazardous.

Crucially, there must always be rescue arrangements in place before anyone enters an enclosed space. This means a trained attendant must remain outside the space at all times, in communication with those inside, with the means to summon help and, if safe to do so, to extract an incapacitated worker. A person who becomes unwell inside an enclosed space may be unable to exit under their own power, and an untrained would-be rescuer who enters without proper equipment may themselves become a victim. The rescue plan must be established, practised and understood by everyone involved before the job starts.

Oxygen-deficient or fume-filled atmospheres can incapacitate a person within seconds of entry. An untrained bystander who sees a colleague collapse inside a manhole and rushes in without breathing apparatus will almost certainly be overcome themselves by the same atmosphere — creating a second casualty. This is why the law requires rescue arrangements to be planned in advance, and why the trained attendant outside the space must summon emergency services rather than attempt an unequipped rescue. In construction, multiple fatalities in a single enclosed-space incident are not uncommon, and the majority of the victims were would-be rescuers. The safest rescue is always one carried out by trained personnel using the correct equipment.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on PPE often ask about employer duties — make sure you cover all three (assess, select, train and supervise) rather than just listing types of PPE. For gas and electricity questions, always name the specific accreditation — Gas Safe for gas; NICEIC for electrical work — and always mention isolation before work begins. For height questions, examiners frequently award marks for naming the specific access methods (MEWP, scaffold, access platform), so learn these terms precisely. For enclosed spaces, the most commonly missed point is the requirement for rescue arrangements — many students write about PPE but forget that a trained attendant and a rescue plan must be in place before anyone enters.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Employers must assess whether PPE is needed, select the correct PPE for each hazard, and train and supervise workers in its proper use, storage and maintenance.
  • Gas work requires Gas Safe registration; electrical work requires NICEIC accreditation. All services must be isolated before work begins, using lock-out/tag-out or valve isolation procedures.
  • Work at height must be planned, use the correct access method (MEWP, scaffold or access platform), account for weather, use inspected equipment, and control risks from fragile surfaces and falling objects.
  • Enclosed spaces carry risks of fumes, reduced oxygen, flooding, fire/explosion and entrapment; rescue arrangements — including a trained attendant outside — must be in place before entry.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the correct accreditation scheme for an electrician carrying out installation work on a construction site?
A) Gas Safe
B) COSHH
C) NICEIC
D) CIOB
State two risks that a worker faces when entering an enclosed space such as a manhole.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: exposure to fumes / reduced oxygen levels / flooding or drowning / fire and explosive atmospheres / entrapment in machinery. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why an employer must train workers in the correct use of PPE, rather than simply providing it.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for stating that PPE only protects the wearer if worn correctly. A second mark for developing this (e.g. a dust mask that is not correctly fitted to the face allows hazardous particles through; a hard hat worn on the back of the head does not protect against falling objects). A third mark for extending the explanation (e.g. training also covers storage and maintenance — PPE that is stored incorrectly or is damaged may be ineffective, and workers must know how and when to replace it). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the safety measures a site manager must put in place before allowing workers to enter an enclosed space.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any four of: carry out a risk assessment identifying the specific hazards in the enclosed space; test the atmosphere using monitoring equipment before entry; provide appropriate PPE such as breathing apparatus if hazardous gases or low oxygen are identified; appoint a trained attendant to remain outside the space throughout; establish rescue arrangements and a rescue plan in advance of entry; ensure workers know how to communicate with the attendant and how to raise an alarm. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A roofing contractor is replacing the roof covering on a two-storey school building. The work will take four weeks. The contractor has told workers to use ladders throughout, without setting up scaffold, to save time and money.

Explain why this approach is unsafe and describe a safer method of access the contractor should use instead.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Explains that using ladders for a four-week roofing project is unsuitable — ladders are only appropriate for short-duration, light work where a three-point contact can be maintained; they do not provide a stable working platform or edge protection for roofing tasks. Identifies the specific risks: falling from the ladder or the roof edge; falling objects landing below; no guardrails or toe-boards protecting workers or people at ground level. Describes a safer method: scaffold with guardrails (handrails and toe-boards) should be erected around the building to give a stable working platform at eaves level; this provides edge protection and prevents falling objects at ground level. Notes that the scaffold must be inspected by a competent person at least every seven days, and that weather conditions must be monitored. Saving time and money does not justify exposing workers to a foreseeable risk of death or serious injury.
Secure (3-4 marks): Identifies that ladders are unsuitable for this task, names a safer access method and gives one or two safety points.
Developing (2 marks): Identifies the hazard but limited explanation of safer alternatives.
Emerging (1 mark): A single basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A maintenance plumber is called to repair a gas boiler and a burst water pipe in the same property. Both jobs require working on live services.

Evaluate the safety steps the plumber must take for each job before and during the work, and explain why Gas Safe registration is particularly important for the gas work.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Evaluates safety steps for the water repair: isolate water supply at the relevant stop valve before work begins; use appropriate PPE (waterproof clothing, safety footwear); check for secondary risks (e.g. water damage to electrical fittings nearby). Evaluates safety steps for the gas repair: must be Gas Safe registered (it is illegal to carry out gas work without this); isolate the gas supply at the meter or isolation valve before starting; follow appropriate working practices and safety procedures for gas; use appropriate PPE; test for gas leaks on completion before restoring supply. Justifies why Gas Safe registration is particularly important: gas leaks can cause explosions, fires and carbon monoxide poisoning — all potentially fatal — and an unregistered person may lack the training to carry out the work safely or to test the system correctly on completion. The requirement for Gas Safe registration exists in law precisely because the consequences of unsafe gas work are catastrophic. A substantiated judgement: both jobs require isolation and PPE, but the gas job carries a higher risk of catastrophic harm, which is why registration and formal accreditation are legally required rather than merely recommended.
Secure (5-6 marks): Both jobs discussed, Gas Safe explained, some evaluation of relative risk.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points for one or both jobs, mostly descriptive.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points, little development. [8 marks]

glossary_terms.definition: Equipment worn by individuals to protect against specific hazards that cannot be adequately controlled by other means, including hard hats, high-visibility vests, safety boots, gloves and dust masks.

A person with the appropriate qualifications, training, experience and accreditations to safely carry out a specific type of work, such as a Gas Safe registered engineer or a NICEIC-approved electrician.
A vehicle-mounted or self-propelled platform that lifts workers to height, such as a cherry picker or scissor lift.

A space that is enclosed or partially enclosed, not designed for continuous human occupancy, and which has a foreseeable risk of serious injury due to hazardous substances, lack of oxygen or other dangerous conditions.
